As it is our last Stated Meeting of the term and for some of us, our last as members, and my final as Speaker, I’d like to say a few words to reflect on our time together over these last four years. In 2021, New Yorkers elected the most diverse and first womenmajority Council in our history, and with it, I was honored to be elected as our city’s first Black Speaker. Our historic representation fully reflected the breadth of New Yorker’s experiences, enabling us to lead differently than our predecessors. When people who have experienced housing insecurity, poverty, working-class struggles, and the impacts of racial and gender disparities come together to represent New Yorkers, we are better prepared to address the perspectives and priorities of everyone in our city. Like CUNY Reconnect, we also created New York State’s first trauma recovery centers in our cities who help Black, Latino and Asian communities receive the support to end cycles of violence which is especially important as these communities have historically lacked access to traditional crime victim services. To address the economic and employment barriers that have contributed to a mental health and workforce shortage, we launched the CUNY Social Work Fellows which will help us improve mental health outcomes, and we created the first city-funded guaranteed income program to help new mothers avoid homelessness, improve maternal health, and reduce child poverty. These have been investments in innovation to confront deeply entrenched inequities. Our city is only as strong as our people, and I’m so proud of how we prioritize New Yorkers over the last four years when chaos in this building was all too present. As public servants, it is our responsibility to improve the conditions of our communities, ensuring that all of us can live healthy, safe, and dignified lives. Today, I am urging my colleagues to vote aye on Intro 1412, the Safer Sanctuary Act. Our sanctuary laws exist for one reason and it’s to keep people safe. Thank you, Majority Leader. We are at a pivotal moment for street vending, and as the daughter and granddaughter of street vendors, I could not be prouder of how far we’ve come. A week ago, I stood at a rally where street vendors were alongside bodegas [sic], restaurants, supermarkets, all side by side calling for one thing, to finally fix our broken vending system. That moment matters because it shows how far we’ve come. When we started, decades’ old license caps made legal compliance nearly impossible for most vendors. Enforcement was inconsistent, ineffective, and stakeholders were so polarized that many feared even sitting at the same table. Vendors felt criminalized. Brick and mortar businesses felt ignored. Reform was stalled. But today’s bill is more balanced with broader brick and mortar support than ever before, and that’s because 431B expands access to licenses, pairing that access with real enforcement, stricter suspension and revocation
